newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine Eurobond announcement seen as premature.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine Eurobond announcement seen as premature.

text.p: Prime Minister Pavlo Lazarenko's announcement on Tuesday that Ukraine would issue its first Eurobond in early May could be optimistic since Ukraine lacks a 1997 budget and a credit rating, analysts said on Tuesday.

"Without a budget, this can't be true, and without a rating they are not able to issue bonds," said Juergen Conrad, an economist at the German Advisory Group on Economic Reforms of Ukraine and at Deutsche Bank Research.
Lazarenko, facing criticism over the sluggish economic reform and talk in the local media of his impending sacking, told parliament that Ukraine would issue the bond soon.
"We will issue foreign (currency denominated) bonds between May 1 and 5," Lazarenko said in reply to a deputy's question.
Earlier he delivered a speech on the former Soviet republic's troubled economy, which has sent teachers and miners into the street protesting against months of unpaid wages.

"In terms of entering the European market -- Eurobonds and Samurai bonds -- I think the first step is completed and we will have the necessary resources by May," he said. Samurai bonds are yen denominated bonds.
But Conrad said parliament first must pass a 1997 budget which meets with International Monetary Fund (IMF) approval and qualify for an IMF three-year, $2.5-$3.0 billion Extended Fund Facility (EFF).
"Without a budget and the IMF money the rating would be so bad that no one would be interested," Conrad said.
The government announced last year it planned a $250 million foreign bond issue by the end of the first quarter.
President Leonid Kuchma, who appointed Lazarenko last June, has strongly urged the largely conservative parliament to pass the budget, and a package of tax reforms to underpin it.
Kuchma will deliver a state of the nation speech on March 21.
Conrad said the EFF would probably not be approved until May, and a rating would take at least a month -- though a number of banks and investment companies were lining up to lead the issue, he added.
Another Western economist said Lazarenko's prediction appeared premature.
"Everyone is saying it will take at least another five or six months," he said.
"Maybe I'm mistaken but they haven't chosen any brokers, although many have been pitching their services to the government. And they have to get a rating from a rating agency."
Local media, quoting unnamed sources, have said Nomura Securities Ltd would lead the issue. Government officials have declined to comment on the reports.
